summary.heading: The photoelectric effect
summary.html:
• Light of high enough frequency on a clean metal surface releases electrons (photoelectrons). Demonstration: ultraviolet discharges a negatively charged zinc plate on an electroscope; bright visible light doesn't.
  • Below the threshold frequency $f_0$: no emission, however bright the light.
  • Above $f_0$: emission is instant, even in dim light.
  • The maximum kinetic energy depends on frequency, not intensity.
  • Brighter light (above $f_0$) gives more electrons per second (a bigger current), not faster ones.
Wave model predictsExperiment shows
Any frequency works if bright enoughNothing below $f_0$
Dim light needs time to build up energyEmission is instant
Brighter light gives faster electrons$E_{\max}$ depends only on $f$

summary.heading: Einstein's photon explanation
summary.html:
$$E_{\max} = hf - \Phi$$
  • Light is a stream of photons, $E = hf$. Each photon gives all its energy to one electron; an electron can't combine energy from two photons.
  • Work function $\Phi$: the minimum energy needed to remove an electron from the surface. Electrons from deeper down lose more energy, so only some have $E_{\max}$.
  • Threshold: $hf_0 = \Phi$, so $f_0 = \dfrac{\Phi}{h}$.
  • This explains all four results: too little energy per photon below $f_0$; one photon is enough above it (instant); more energy per photon at higher $f$; more photons per second in brighter light.

summary.heading: Stopping voltage and the graph of maximum kinetic energy against frequency
summary.html:
$$eV_s = E_{\max} = hf - \Phi$$
  • Reversing the supply in a photocell repels the electrons. At the stopping voltage $V_s$ even the fastest are turned back and the current is zero. In eV: $V_s = 0.68$ V means $E_{\max} = 0.68$ eV.
  • Brighter light of the same frequency: bigger current, same $V_s$. Higher frequency: bigger $V_s$. At large forward p.d. the current levels off (every electron is collected).
  • Graph of $E_{\max}$ against $f$: a straight line. Gradient = $h$ (the same for every metal); $f$-intercept = $f_0$; extended $E$-intercept = $-\Phi$.
  • Plotting $V_s$ against $f$ gives gradient $\dfrac{h}{e}$ (Millikan's measurement of $h$).

summary.heading: Matter waves and electron diffraction
summary.html:
$$\lambda = \frac{h}{p} = \frac{h}{mv}$$
  • De Broglie: every moving particle has a wavelength. Photons obey the same rule, so a photon has momentum $p = \dfrac{h}{\lambda}$.
  • Everyday objects have far too much momentum for a detectable wavelength. Electrons accelerated through a few hundred volts have $\lambda \approx 10^{-10}$ m, about the atomic spacing in crystals.
  • From an accelerating p.d.: $E_k = eV$, then $p = \sqrt{2mE_k}$, then $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p}$.
  • Electron diffraction through thin graphite gives rings (maxima and minima from interference): evidence for the wave nature of matter. A higher accelerating voltage gives smaller rings.
  • High-energy electrons scattered by nuclei show a central maximum and a first minimum at $\sin\theta \approx \dfrac{\lambda}{D}$, where $D$ is the diameter of the nucleus. This is how nuclear sizes are measured.

summary.heading: Compton scattering
summary.html:
$$\Delta\lambda = \lambda_f - \lambda_i = \frac{h}{m_ec}(1 - \cos\theta)$$
  • X-rays or gamma rays scattered by (effectively free) electrons come off with a longer wavelength. A wave would keep its wavelength.
  • Explanation: a photon with energy and momentum collides with one electron; the electron recoils, so the scattered photon has less energy. Energy and momentum are both conserved.
  • $\dfrac{h}{m_ec} = 2.43 \times 10^{-12}$ m. Shift 0 at $\theta = 0$, $\dfrac{h}{m_ec}$ at 90°, greatest ($2\dfrac{h}{m_ec}$) at 180°. No derivation needed.
  • Only noticeable for X-rays and gamma rays. Stronger evidence for photons than the photoelectric effect: it shows they carry momentum.

summary.heading: Wave–particle duality
summary.html:
Wave behaviourParticle behaviour
Lightinterference, diffraction, polarizationphotoelectric effect, Compton scattering, line spectra
Electronselectron diffractiondeflection by fields, definite charge and mass, tracks in detectors
  • Neither picture is complete on its own: waves describe how light and matter travel; particles describe how they interact, in single events.
  • $E = hf$ and $p = \dfrac{h}{\lambda}$ link the particle quantities to the wave quantities.

summary.heading: Watch out for
summary.html:
• Saying brighter light gives faster photoelectrons.
  • Confusing the work function (an energy) with the threshold frequency.
  • Mixing eV and J in $E_{\max} = hf - \Phi$.
  • Saying all photoelectrons have $E_{\max}$.
  • Putting kinetic energy into $\lambda = \dfrac{h}{p}$ instead of momentum.
  • Thinking the Compton shift depends on the incident wavelength: it depends only on the angle.

Paradigm shift: Why was the wave model of light so hard to give up in 1905? List the evidence that supported it.
Planck himself resisted the photon. Does a paradigm shift need the old generation to be convinced, or to retire?
Falsification: Millikan set out to disprove Einstein's equation and confirmed it. What does that say about the value of trying to prove a theory wrong?
Which single photoelectric observation would you choose as the strongest falsification of the pure wave model, and why?
Creativity: De Broglie's idea came largely from a sense of symmetry. Is a hunch like that a legitimate starting point in science?
What turned de Broglie's guess into accepted physics?
Experiments: Why did Compton's result persuade people who doubted the photoelectric explanation?
Design question: what would you measure, and at which angles, to test the Compton equation?

oracy.html:
Opinion line (whole class, 8 minutes): students stand between "agree" and "disagree", explain their place, and may move after hearing others. Claim: "Shining brighter light on a metal surface makes the photoelectrons come off with more kinetic energy."

  • I'm standing here because …
  • I moved after hearing …, because …
  • That would only be true if …

Listen for: intensity sets the number of photons per second, so more electrons, not faster ones; $E_{\max} = hf - \Phi$ depends only on frequency, and below the threshold frequency none are emitted.

Can two contradictory models both be tru: Is light "really" a wave or a particle, or is the question badly posed?
Find an example from another subject where two incompatible descriptions are both useful (a map projection, two historical accounts).
Does an experiment decide what we see?: Ask students: if you only ever did diffraction experiments, what would you conclude light is?
How much does the design of an experiment shape the knowledge it produces?
Why do scientists resist new ideas?: List reasons a scientist might reject the photon idea in 1905 that were sensible at the time.
When does scepticism become stubbornness? Can students suggest a test for telling them apart?
What counts as understanding?: Students can calculate $E_{\max}$ without picturing a photon. Do they understand the photoelectric effect?
Is being able to predict results enough, or must a theory also give a picture of what is happening?
